metadata.title: Enterprise Architecture Management Platform Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how an enterprise architecture platform would need to change when the company is split apart, AI oversight becomes a board obligation, an acquisition brings incompatible architecture evidence, or a regulated AI business must be separated under all three conditions.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: Architects maintain one enterprise metamodel, import application and technology records into a shared repository, map ownership and dependencies, publish roadmaps, and use current-state views for portfolio and governance decisions. The design assumes the enterprise boundary, ownership model, classification rules, and source semantics remain sufficiently stable for one authoritative model.
metadata.residualArchitecture: The changed design treats legal entities, operating units, capabilities, applications, services, data, AI models, owners, consumers, controls, source assertions, decisions, and transition states as separate versioned records. Evidence keeps its source, meaning, observation time, confidence, and access policy, so a business can be split, acquired evidence can coexist before reconciliation, and regulated AI assets can move without erasing obligations or decision history.
metadata.note: These tests attack the business boundary and governance assumptions behind the repository. The important change is not a larger diagram: it is the ability to preserve ownership, evidence, obligations, and decisions while the meaning and shape of the enterprise change.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: The board announces that the enterprise will split into three independent companies within nine months
stressors.detection: Board decision, transaction perimeter, legal-entity plan, transition-service agreements, application and data ownership workshops, supplier contracts, regulatory approvals, and separation milestones.
stressors.attractor: Applications, capabilities, data, contracts, people, and controls that looked like one portfolio must be owned, shared, duplicated, retired, or temporarily supplied across new legal boundaries. A single owner and target state per object can no longer describe the operating reality or the transition.
stressors.businessReaction: Define each company's required capabilities and obligations, identify shared dependencies, decide ownership and service arrangements, sequence separations, fund replacements, govern temporary exceptions, and prove that every new company can operate on day one.
stressors.residue: Separate legal entity, operating unit, capability need, asset ownership, service consumption, data responsibility, contract, control, transition service, target state, milestone, and decision. Every relationship is effective-dated, so one application can move from shared service to duplicated or replaced states without rewriting its history.

impacts.effect: Transformation leadership can govern a moving enterprise boundary instead of treating the current organization chart as permanent.
The separation portfolio can coordinate capability, application, data, contract, control, and ownership dependencies.
Impact analysis compares separation options and exposes shared services, stranded costs, obligations, and day-one gaps.
Dependency readiness requires a confirmed owner on both sides of each temporary and future-state relationship.
Adds transaction perimeters, effective-dated ownership, transition services, separation waves, and day-one readiness.
Plans the organizational split as linked capability, asset, service, contract, and control transitions.
Shows cross-company dependencies and how each changes across separation milestones.
Versions current, transition, day-one, and end-state architectures for each resulting company.
Links funded separation initiatives to the precise relationships and obligations they must change.
Owns the separation decision model with corporate development, business, technology, finance, legal, security, and data leaders.
Makes effective-dated carve-out and transition architecture a portfolio-management benchmark.

stressors.name: New regulation makes the board accountable for every consequential AI system and its evidence
stressors.detection: Final regulation and guidance, regulator inquiries, internal AI discovery, procurement records, model and data inventories, architecture reviews, incidents, control testing, and board reporting requests.
stressors.attractor: AI features are embedded inside applications and vendor services but ownership, intended use, model versions, training or grounding data, affected decisions, controls, and exceptions are scattered. A static application catalog cannot show which regulated obligations apply or whether a release remains approved.
stressors.businessReaction: Discover AI uses, classify their consequence and legal scope, assign accountable owners, connect models and data to business decisions, define controls and human oversight, stop unapproved changes, document exceptions, and give the board current evidence of readiness.
stressors.residue: Add a governed AI-use record separate from application, feature, model, provider, model version, data source, business decision, affected group, jurisdiction, owner, control, evaluation, human review, incident, exception, and release. Approval applies to a specific combination and expires when a material input changes.

impacts.effect: Technology governance covers the actual AI use and affected decision, not merely the vendor or application name.
Risk leaders can find, assess, approve, monitor, and explain consequential AI changes before release.
Assessment joins purpose, model, data, affected parties, jurisdiction, evaluation, controls, review, and release evidence.
An AI system counts as governed only when the current use, model, data, owner, controls, and approval are connected.
Adds AI-use classification, control obligations, approval scope, release gates, exceptions, and board evidence.
Turns AI discovery and review into an operating governance flow linked to every material change.
Evaluates each AI use against jurisdiction, consequence, policy, ownership, and change triggers.
Maps required controls and human oversight to the specific AI use, model, data, and decision.
Preserves evaluations, approvals, releases, monitoring, incidents, exceptions, and board evidence.
Owns the governance record with AI product, data, legal, security, risk, architecture, and business-accountability teams.
Makes living AI-use and control traceability a modern architecture-governance benchmark.

stressors.name: An acquisition closes with an incompatible architecture model and contradictory ownership data
stressors.detection: Deal close, acquired repositories and spreadsheets, source-system imports, conflicting identifiers and taxonomies, duplicate applications, ownership disputes, stale records, integration planning, and architect review.
stressors.attractor: Forcing both companies into one metamodel creates false matches and loses local meaning; keeping two disconnected repositories prevents dependency, cost, risk, and integration decisions. Declaring one source authoritative before reconciliation turns uncertainty into misleading certainty.
stressors.businessReaction: Preserve both evidence sets, map equivalent and disputed concepts, assign stewards, identify high-value decisions, reconcile only what those decisions require, expose conflicts and freshness, and improve the combined model through reviewed assertions rather than a one-time migration.
stressors.residue: Separate a real-world architecture object from source record, source schema, local identifier, assertion, observation time, confidence, steward, semantic mapping, conflict, and reviewed resolution. Multiple claims can coexist until a decision resolves them, while shared views explain what is known, disputed, or stale.

impacts.effect: A living architecture model can admit uncertainty and conflicting evidence while still supporting decisions.
Architecture leaders can federate acquired evidence without pretending that incompatible records already agree.
Integration preserves source meaning, mappings, conflicts, confidence, and stewardship alongside normalized views.
Validation distinguishes complete reviewed assertions from mechanically populated but unresolved records.
Adds federated schemas, source assertions, semantic mappings, conflicts, confidence, and review state.
Treats acquisition integration as continuing evidence reconciliation rather than one destructive import.
Maps local concepts to shared concepts without erasing the source schema or disputed semantics.
Retains source identity, timestamps, changes, failures, and reconciliation status for every assertion.
Measures freshness, completeness, conflict, confidence, and decision fitness separately.
Owns semantic federation with acquired-company architects, source owners, portfolio teams, and decision makers.
Makes explainable multi-model federation and post-merger evidence quality a platform benchmark.

stressors.name: A regulator orders the rapid sale of an acquired AI-heavy business unit during the corporate split
stressors.detection: Regulatory order, sale perimeter, acquired source assertions, AI-use inventory, legal entities, application and data dependencies, controls, contracts, transition services, bidders, and separation deadlines.
stressors.attractor: The company must prove what belongs to the unit, which AI and data obligations travel with it, which evidence is trustworthy, what remains shared temporarily, and what cannot cross the new boundary. A flat repository cannot answer without either exposing restricted evidence or silently dropping dependencies.
stressors.businessReaction: Create an evidence-backed sale perimeter, resolve only decision-critical conflicts, identify AI and data obligations, assign every dependency to transfer, replace, retire, or transition service, restrict bidder access, approve day-one controls, and preserve a complete decision record.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: effective-dated enterprise boundaries describe the sale and transition, governed AI-use records carry their controls and evidence, and federated source assertions expose conflicts without losing provenance. Existing decision and access controls compose the divestiture view.

impacts.effect: Executives receive a defensible sale perimeter with costs, risks, controls, dependencies, and unresolved evidence visible.
Portfolio leaders can decide what transfers, remains, is replaced, or is temporarily serviced without losing accountability.
The decision pack distinguishes verified facts, disputed assertions, regulatory obligations, and approved transition assumptions.
A decision pack is accepted only when its perimeter, evidence quality, AI obligations, and transition dependencies are explicit.
Composes governed sale views for executives, architects, risk reviewers, transaction teams, and restricted bidders.
Reuses the existing boundary, AI-governance, and evidence models to assess the regulated divestiture.
Calculates transfer and remaining-company impact across assets, services, data, controls, and milestones.
Records perimeter decisions, evidence, conditions, owners, exceptions, and expiry dates.
Presents role-appropriate readiness and unresolved decisions without leaking restricted sale evidence.
Coordinates stakeholder views and controlled evidence access across the transaction and architecture teams.
Makes rapid regulated carve-out decisions a visible enterprise-transformation benchmark.
